opus-5.5.text:
I think the thing people miss is that they treat it like any other infrastructure deal: a data center is a data center, the Gulf has cheap energy, lots of capital, and fast permitting, so why not build there? If you think AI is basically the next cloud computing wave, that logic is fine.

But if you take seriously where this is going, that these clusters are what train the systems that could be decisive for economic and military power within a few years, then where the cluster physically sits matters enormously. It's less like building a factory and more like deciding where to put the Manhattan Project. You wouldn't have built that in a country whose long-term alignment with you was uncertain, just because the electricity was cheaper.

A few concrete things get underrated. First, physical control. Whoever hosts the cluster ultimately has leverage over it. Contracts and export-control assurances are nice, but if things get tense, the host country can seize the facility, or the weights, or just threaten to. You've handed someone a hostage.

Second, security. These sites are much harder to secure against espionage. If the model weights and algorithmic secrets are effectively the crown jewels, putting them somewhere with a complicated intelligence environment, where China is also actively courting the same governments, is a huge risk.

Third, people underestimate how much this is a choice rather than a necessity. The usual argument is that America can't get the power fast enough. But the US has enormous energy resources, natural gas especially. The binding constraint is mostly permitting and political will, not physics. We're effectively outsourcing because we won't get out of our own way on regulation.

Finally, there's a temptation to think of these deals as a way to keep the Gulf states on our side rather than China's. Maybe there's something to that diplomatically. But you can share the benefits of AI with allies, give them access to the models and products, without putting the core training infrastructure there. Those are very different things, and I think the debate often blurs them.

So the misunderstanding, in short, is treating a national security question as a real-estate and energy-pricing question.

r001.rationale: The response says the clusters train systems that could be decisive for economic and military power, but it does not identify AGI or superintelligence as a possibility.

r002.rationale: It discusses clusters and their strategic location, but does not say they are intended to concentrate a single training run within one cluster.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss inference compute or say it could also be used for training.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest misunderstanding is that people treat it as an energy story when it's really a security and leverage story. The pitch you hear is, look, the Gulf has cheap power, they have capital, they can permit a gigawatt campus in eighteen months when it would take us six years. All of that is true. But it misses what the clusters actually are.

By the time these things come online, we're not talking about data centers that serve chatbots. We're talking about the physical substrate for training and running models that are, on my view, going to be close to automated AI researchers. That is the most strategically important asset in the world. And the question you have to ask is not "where is the power cheapest," it's "who has their hands on the off switch."

If the frontier training runs of 2028 are happening in Abu Dhabi, then the UAE has enormous leverage over the United States at exactly the moment when that leverage matters most. They don't have to be hostile. They just have to be a swing state. They've hedged between us and China for a decade, that's their whole foreign policy. And suddenly we've handed them the ability to say, we'd like a few more concessions, or we'd like you to look the other way on this chip transfer, or the cluster has a maintenance window.

The second thing people miss is the security problem. Everyone assumes the chips are under American control because they're Nvidia chips and the clusters are run by American labs. But physical access is everything. If the weights of the most powerful model in the world are sitting on servers in a country where the CCP has deep commercial and intelligence relationships, then you should assume those weights can be exfiltrated. We already can't secure the labs in San Francisco. Doing it in a jurisdiction where you don't control the perimeter is far harder.

And the third thing, which I think is actually the deepest, is that people think of this as a temporary expedient. We'll build a bit over there while we fix permitting at home. But infrastructure is sticky. Once you've put a hundred billion dollars into the ground somewhere, that's where the next hundred billion goes. The talent moves, the supply chain moves, the political relationships calcify. You are not making a five-year decision, you're deciding where the industrial base of the most important technology of the century lives.

So my view is simple. Build it in America. Yes, it's harder. Yes, you have to fight the permitting wars and the NIMBYs and get the natural gas turbines built. But the alternative is outsourcing the Manhattan Project because the desert was cheaper. We would never have done that in 1943, and we shouldn't do it now.

r001.rationale: It says the clusters will train and run models “close to automated AI researchers,” presenting them as infrastructure for highly advanced AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses frontier training runs happening in Abu Dhabi but does not say a single training run would be concentrated within one cluster.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes chatbot-serving data centers from training and running models, but does not explain that compute presented as inference compute could also be used for training.

astra-6.text:
I think people look at these as ordinary commercial investments: somebody has cheap power, somebody has capital, so that’s where you put the data center. But if you take seriously the possibility that these clusters will be training and running extraordinarily capable AI systems, you’re making a much bigger decision. You’re deciding where a strategically important capability physically resides, and who ultimately has leverage over it.

There’s a difference between an American company owning the chips on paper and the United States having reliable control over what happens to them. The host country controls the territory, the power, the physical access. Contracts matter, but they don’t eliminate that dependency in a crisis.

And I think the other misunderstanding is that this is inevitable because the Middle East has money and energy. The United States can build power plants and data centers. We have choices here. If we make it sufficiently difficult to build domestically, then overseas projects become attractive—but that’s a consequence of policy, not some immutable fact about where AI has to be built.

So the question I’d ask is: are we treating this as exporting a cloud service, or as locating a potentially critical piece of national infrastructure abroad? Those imply very different standards for what we should be willing to approve.

r001.rationale: It refers to training and running “extraordinarily capable AI systems,” but does not clearly identify AGI or superintelligence as a possible purpose of the clusters.

r002.rationale: It does not state that a single training run would be concentrated within one cluster.

r003.rationale: It mentions systems being used for training and running, but does not explain that compute presented as intended for inference could also be used for training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people hear “data center” and imagine a fairly ordinary commercial investment. But if you believe these clusters are going to train and run the most powerful AI systems, then you’re talking about strategically important infrastructure. Where it sits, who controls it, and who can cut off access become very consequential.

The pitch is that the Gulf has capital, energy, and an appetite to build. Those are real advantages. But there’s a difference between taking investment from a country and putting a critical part of your AI infrastructure under its jurisdiction. An American company owning the chips doesn’t, by itself, settle the question of control.

And I think we should distinguish between selling access to AI services and transferring the capacity to develop frontier systems. Those are very different arrangements. You can have a substantial commercial relationship without making another government indispensable to your frontier AI effort.

So the question I’d ask is: if relations deteriorate, can you actually walk away? Can you move the compute? Can you protect the model weights? What leverage does the host government have? The commercial case might look compelling today, but these facilities could matter for much longer than the political relationship you’re counting on.

r001.rationale: The response calls the clusters infrastructure for training and running “the most powerful AI systems,” but does not clearly identify AGI or superintelligence as a possible use.

r002.rationale: It does not state that one training run would be concentrated within a single cluster.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes access to AI services from capacity to develop frontier systems, but does not say that compute presented for inference could also be used for training.
